title: THE PATIENT VERDICT — WARDROOM
intro:
The wardroom is a table bolted to a deck and six chairs, five of which nobody
has sat in for eleven weeks.

Interrogator Dmetri Vaux has two years of paper laid out on it in order, with
the tabs turned the right way for somebody reading from your side.

He has been setting it out for about an hour. He is standing.
revisit: The wardroom. A bolted table, six chairs, and a man who will not use one.

objects.careful:
The last third is in a different ink.

He ran out. Somewhere in the second year, in a study on tier four, working on his own time on a case he could never file, Interrogator Dmetri Vaux ran out of ink and went and bought more and carried on, and the join is at the eleventh month, and there is no note about it because who would he be noting it for.

The conclusion is three lines and it is wrong.

Everything above the conclusion is correct.

objects.careless: Six chairs bolted round a table. One of them is yours. Five of them have not been sat in for eleven weeks.
objects.careful:
One of them is worn at the arms in the way a chair is worn by one man over nineteen years.

It is at the head, which is where a master sits, and Vaux is standing next to it and has been for an hour, and there is a version of this conversation where he sits down in it and it is not this one and both of you know it.

npcs.title: Interrogator Dmetri Vaux
npcs.topic_refusal: "Ask," Vaux says. "I have stopped deciding in advance which things I'll answer."
npcs.portrait:
Interrogator Dmetri Vaux, sixty-one, in a wardroom four days out, with two years of paper laid out on the table in order.

He is standing. He has not sat down in front of you once.
npcs.greeting:
The dossier is already out when you come in. All of it, in order, squared, with the tabs turned the right way for somebody reading from your side of the table.

He has been setting it out for about an hour.

"Sit down," Vaux says. "I'm not going to. This will take you forty minutes and I have found that I would rather be on my feet for it."
npcs.reprise: He stands at the head of the table with the paper squared.
deflect: He squares a page that is already square.

topics.text:
Forty minutes.

It is the best piece of investigative work anybody in the Adamant Crown has done in a decade and you have read it before, in a wax vault, in a hurry, and you have never read it *properly*.

Twenty-six months. Every elevation, transfer and quiet retirement Yolanda Crase has signed since 820, cross-indexed against the four offices that hold the countersignatures, with the eleven cases where the countersigning seat is the same seat marked in a second hand because he ran out of the first ink.

Every date checks. Every requisition number checks. He has been honest about the two places where he could not get the paper and has written what he inferred and marked it as inference.

And at the end of it, in a conclusion three lines long, he has her as the author.

"Two years," Vaux says. "Every hour I wasn't on duty. I had her at the centre of it."

"You had her at the centre of it because she *is* at the centre of it."

"I had her as the *author*." He squares a page that is already square. "There is a difference between a hand and a pen, and I have spent two years interrogating a pen."

[ C10 HELD ]

"I want to apologise to you and I want to be precise about what for, because an imprecise apology is a way of asking to be argued with."

He does not look away at any point.

"It is not for obstructing you in the first week. That was correct. A records-adept with eleven years in had been handed a rosette by the woman who signed the elevation and I would have been derelict not to obstruct you, and I would do it again tomorrow.

"It is for forty years of being right about small things."

He lets that sit.

"I checked his forms. I found his errors — there were four in nineteen years and I found all four and I was *pleased* about it. I was a good clerk to a man who needed a witness.

"He chose you because you were not a good clerk."

A long pause.

"I have spent eleven weeks being bitter about that and about four days understanding it, and the understanding took place on this hull, out here, where nothing is reading over my shoulder, which I do not think is a coincidence and which I would rather you did not comment on."

You tell him he was right.

Not about the author — about her. That she is at the centre of it, that she has been at the centre of it since 820, that every road out of the fourth hour of the first morning runs through her office, and that a man who assembled twenty-six months of that on his own time and got the conclusion wrong is a man who was one word out.

"One word," Vaux says.

"One word."

"It is the *only* word." But something has come off him. He sits down, which he has not done in front of you once, and looks at the paper for a while.

"Thank you. I am going to be insufferable about that at some point and I would like it noted that I know."

At Cantica-Null he is going to speak first, before she does, and it is going to cost her the opening, and neither of you knows that yet.

[ VERITY +1 ]

"Because you would have got yourself killed in the Vault in the first week," Vaux says, "and then who would I have argued with."

He means it as a deflection and it comes out as the other thing, and he hears it, and does not correct it, which for him is an enormous concession.

Then, in a different voice:

"Also because I am sixty-one and I have one piece of physical paper left that matters and there is nowhere in the Vardan sector I could have left it. Not a bank, not a seat, not a Conclave office. I have spent forty years learning exactly how many places there are in this sector where a document is safe, and the answer, as it turns out, is that there is one, and it is a coat."

"You have not been down to the hold," Vaux says. It is not a reproach; it is
the first item on a list.

"He recites in the corridor. He has been reciting in the corridor since the
second day and nobody has asked him to and he is not doing it at anybody. I
have been writing it down."

He produces about nine pages. The hand is worse than his usual hand, because
most of it was taken standing up.

"Compliant worlds, cycle 087: thirty-three. He has said it eleven times and it
is thirty-three every time. The tithe grades are in here and the district
counts are not, because he does those faster than I write."

"You should have told me."

"You should have gone down to the hold." He squares the pages. "I am not a
savant, Inquisitor. This is nine pages of a man in a corridor as heard by a
sixty-one-year-old with a pen, and there is not one word of it I could swear to
in front of anybody, and I want that understood before you put it in your
coat."

[ C9b HELD ]

acts.text:
"One thing," Vaux says. "Then I'll stop and you can go and be somewhere else.

"Whatever you decide at the end of this — and I have read enough of it to know there is going to be a decision and that it is going to be worse than any of us are expecting — I would like to be told first. In words. To my face. Not on a form, not through the retinue, and not by finding out."

"That's all?"

"That is the entire remainder of what I want from my career."

You give him your word, standing, in a wardroom, four days out from anywhere.

Vaux nods once and then takes something out of his coat that he has plainly been carrying since Vardan Prime: a sealed courier writ, physical, Ordo, made out to a Conclave seat and signed by a man who has been dead eleven weeks.

"His dead-man channel. He gave it to me in 'ninety-one and told me to use it if he ever stopped writing to me, and he stopped writing to me eleven weeks ago and I have not used it, because I could not work out who to send."

He puts it on the paper.

"That is one sealed physical channel out of this sector that does not pass through a cogitator. There is not another. Do not spend it on being right."

[ VAUX_APOLOGY — CONCLAVE_CHANNEL ]

You will not promise it.

There are good reasons. You do not know what the decision is going to be, you do not know who will be in the room, and a promise made four days out to a man who has been wrong about the biggest thing in his professional life is a promise you may have to break in front of him.

Vaux takes it well, which is the worst available outcome.

"That is a reasonable position," he says. "I would have taken it myself at your age and I would have been just as right about it."

He squares the paper and begins putting it away, tab by tab, in order.

Whatever he had in his coat stays in his coat. He does not mention it and you do not know it is there, and it will be there at Cantica-Null, and it will still be there afterwards.

exits.text: Out of the wardroom. He is still putting the paper away, tab by tab, in order.

C10.label: Vaux's hand-kept dossier on Crase — twenty-six months, correct in every particular, one word wrong in its conclusion
C10.file_text:
FILED. CLASS: DISCIPLINARY / UNAUTHORISED SURVEILLANCE OF A SUPERIOR OFFICER. INDEXED. ATTRIBUTED: VAUX, D., INTERROGATOR.

The cogitator files it against the standing personnel roll, correctly, in nine
seconds.

It is out of relay range and will transmit at the next waypoint, where the
countersigning authority is the subject of the document.
C10.note_text:
Copied out over four days, by hand, from a hull's wardroom table.

Every elevation, transfer and quiet retirement she has signed since 820,
cross-indexed to four offices, with the eleven where the countersigning seat is
the same seat.

The last third is in a different ink because he ran out.

The conclusion is wrong by one word and the word is *author*.

C9b.label: Vaux's transcription of Fenn's recitation — nine pages, taken standing up in a corridor, and not a word of it he could swear to
C9b.file_text:
FILED. CLASS: SAVANT OUTPUT / PROJECTION, TRANSCRIBED. INDEXED. ATTRIBUTED: VAUX, D., INTERROGATOR.

The cogitator files it against the savant's personnel record and appends,
correctly, that the transcription is secondhand and unattested.

It is a good filing of a document that is worth exactly what it says it is
worth.
C9b.note_text:
Nine pages in a hand that gets worse down the page, copied out again in mine.

Thirty-three at cycle 087, said eleven times, always thirty-three. The tithe
grades. No district counts.

He wrote at the top, before he gave it to me: *heard, not held.*

strings.no_such_thing: A table, six chairs, and two years of somebody else's paper.
strings.already_read: You have looked twice. He is waiting for you to reach the conclusion.
strings.no_terminal: There is no relay within nine days of this hull, which is why he is talking.
strings.read_room_locked: Nobody arranged a wardroom. He arranged the table.
